final_proof:
Let ψ = φ⁻¹ : A₂ → A₁. Since φ is a bijection, ψ exists and is a bijection: it is surjective because every x ∈ A₁ satisfies x = ψ(φ(x)), and it is injective because ψ(y) = ψ(z) implies, after applying φ, that y = z. It remains to prove that ψ is a complete lattice homomorphism.

For i ∈ {1,2}, denote joins and meets in Lᵢ by ⋁ᵢ and ⋀ᵢ, respectively. Let T be an arbitrary subset of A₂ (possibly empty), and put S = ψ[T] ⊆ A₁. The inverse identities imply φ[S] = T: if s ∈ S, then s = ψ(t) for some t ∈ T and therefore φ(s) = t ∈ T; conversely, each t ∈ T is φ(ψ(t)), with ψ(t) ∈ S.

Because φ is a complete lattice homomorphism, it preserves the join of every subset of A₁. Consequently,

φ(⋁₁ S) = ⋁₂ φ[S] = ⋁₂ T.

Applying ψ to this equality and using ψ ∘ φ = id_A₁ gives

ψ(⋁₂ T) = ⋁₁ S = ⋁₁ ψ[T].

Thus ψ preserves arbitrary joins. Likewise, preservation of arbitrary meets by φ gives

φ(⋀₁ S) = ⋀₂ φ[S] = ⋀₂ T,

and applying ψ gives

ψ(⋀₂ T) = ⋀₁ S = ⋀₁ ψ[T].

Thus ψ preserves arbitrary meets as well. Since T was arbitrary and the argument also applies to T = ∅, it includes the empty join and empty meet (hence preservation of the bottom and top elements). Therefore ψ = φ⁻¹ : L₂ → L₁ is a bijective complete lattice homomorphism.
